It includes the remains of Naga people taken during the colonial era and held at the museum for decades.

Advertisement Since 2020, the museum has worked with the FNR and RRaD teams, tribal Hohos, elders, churches and communities across the Naga homeland to decide how the ancestors should be cared for and returned.
The Forum for Naga Reconciliation approached the museum earlier this year to seek the return of the ancestral remains.

Since 2020, the museum has worked with the FNR and RRaD teams, tribal Hohos, elders, churches and communities across the Naga homeland to decide how the ancestors should be cared for and returned, according to PTI.
"In February 2026, the University of Oxford received a claim from the FNR for 40 ancestral remains kept in the Pitt Rivers Museum.
The claim followed the university's procedures for the return of cultural objects and was agreed by the Oxford University Council on July 13, 2026," the museum said.

After the ceremony, the ancestors will finally return home, accompanied by a Naga delegation, including leaders and elders of several Naga tribe Hohos, together with members of the FNR and RRaD," the museum said.
A 30-member delegation from Nagaland received the remains at a ceremony in Oxford on Monday.

advertisement ❮ ❯ Read Full Story "I feel honoured that we walked alongside our partners to find the path to return for these 39 Naga ancestors, who have been away from their homeland for far too long," said Professor Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum.
The museum holds the world's largest collection of Naga material, much of it gathered by colonial administrators in the early 20th century.
The council approved the return of 39 ancestral remains but declined to return one other remain because it did not have a "clear provenance as Naga".
Most of the Naga remains in the collection were brought to Oxford by Hutton and another administrator-anthropologist, James Philip Mills, between 1910 and 1940.
The return was supported by the Homebound Project, which funds the repatriation of ancestral remains and cultural belongings from UK institutions to Indigenous communities.
The 39 Naga ancestors will now be taken to India and laid to rest beneath a joint memorial in Nagaland.
Most of the remains are skulls and will be given a "respectful rest", according to Naga tribal leaders, who plan to bury them beneath a joint memorial in a park in Nagaland.
The remains were displayed at the museum until 2020, when it removed all human remains from public display.
Especially inspiring is the beautiful way that collective work and shared action kept engagement growing to become a Naga-wide movement of healing and unification," Van Broekhoven said.
"Following this decision, the Pitt Rivers Museum has been working closely with the Nagas to agree on a date for the handover ceremony.
